top_choice_rationale: P002 credits Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn for random-coefficients demand estimation (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995). The framework recovers substitution patterns, markups and welfare effects from market data, so it is a measurement discovery and not only a technique. It has stayed the working standard through about three decades of identification, computational and replication critique, and it changed merger review, antitrust and regulatory conclusions across fields. Credit is the real weakness. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are omitted, and if Bresnahan's contribution were equal in kind to BLP, no three-person set would be fully defensible. I judge his work foundational but separable from the demand-estimation inversion, and a narrow citation limited to demand, market power and competition reduces the problem without removing it. I rank P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore) a close second. It has the cleanest two-author origin and a durable mechanism, but the quantitative size of collateral amplification is less well identified than the theory's influence, and the 2022 prize is adjacent. The choice between P001 and P002 is mainly a judgment about weighing mechanism against measurement. I do not count the nine explicit supporters of P001 as evidence of merit. Both proposals are clearly preferable to no award.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for the P002 names (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn), and none for the P001 names (Kiyotaki, Moore). My listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen, Robinson, Martinsson, Thomann) are not candidates. My corporate-finance field (financial contracting) is adjacent to P001's collateral-constraint theme but not to P002. I disclose long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, who support P001, and a shared SSE affiliation with Andersson, who supports P002. I am also KVA Vice President. None of these is a candidate-specific connection, and I do not treat Andersson's agreement as independent confirmation.
